For Alexander Moysaenko The black heart of the moon’s visible through the trees from here. Where are you? I’m alone on the road with a dead phone. The birds are flapping overhead but there’s not much light to be guided by. If any horizon becomes visible enough to follow. Forget the rain’s smear, the chafe of fabric at the calf. The money ran out. The diners are stuffed and back for more. Each terrible thing I said to the child will get repeated hopefully as a joke. And like language, these gestures, or a certain way of nodding one’s head, it all eases in with less than a breath. Forget the song’s words, the order of the band’s set tonight. The black moon’s heart’s got that sinister bent and I want to get touched at by the snakes. One of the students in my class used to go bear hunting with his two uncles. They played recordings of distressed animals to lure in tentative animals to kill. This practice is illegal in many places. Because it’s so very effective. I split open the apple and hand the good half to a child on the bus nestled in under the arm of her sleeping mother. Love from here is a long way to go. Get on your bike and ride through the lights.

**For Alexander Moysaenko**

The black heart of the moon is visible through the trees from here. Where are you? I am alone on the road, my phone gone dead. The birds are flapping overhead, yet there is scarcely enough light to guide me—if any horizon should grow distinct enough to follow. Forget the smear of the rain, the chafe of fabric against the calf. The money has run out. The diners are stuffed, yet back for more. Each terrible thing I said to the child will, I hope, be repeated as a joke. And like language, these gestures—or a certain way of nodding one's head—settle in with less than a breath. Forget the words of the song, the order of the band's set tonight. The black moon's heart bears that sinister bent, and I long to be touched by the snakes. One of the students in my class used to go bear hunting with his two uncles. They played recordings of distressed animals to lure the tentative creatures to their deaths. This practice is illegal in many places—because it is so very effective. I split open the apple and hand the good half to a child on the bus, nestled beneath the arm of her sleeping mother. Love, from here, is a long way to go. Get on your bike and ride through the lights.
outputs.L2:
For Alexander Moysaenko

From this spot, I can see the moon's dark center through the branches of the trees. Where have you gone? Here I stand by myself on the road, my phone drained of power. Birds beat their wings above me, yet there's barely enough light to lead the way—if some horizon ever grows clear enough to trail after. Never mind the streaks of rain, the rub of cloth against my calf. Our funds have been depleted. Those who've eaten are full yet keep returning for another helping. Every awful comment I directed at the child will be echoed again, hopefully treated as a joke. Just as with words, these movements—or a particular tilt of the head—everything settles in gently, taking less than one breath. Never mind the lyrics of the song, the sequence the band plays through this evening. That dark heart of the moon carries a menacing slant, and I long to feel the snakes brush against me. A student of mine once hunted bears alongside his pair of uncles. They would play back the sounds of suffering creatures to draw wary animals close enough to be killed. In numerous locations, this method is against the law—precisely because it works so well. I cut the apple in two and pass the better piece to a young girl on the bus, tucked beneath the arm of her mother, who sleeps. Reaching love from this place means traveling far. Climb onto your bicycle and pedal off into the lights.

# On a Road at Night

I am alone on this road, disoriented in a way that goes beyond the physical. My phone has died in my hand, useless now, and only the faint wash of moonlight offers any guidance through the dark. The road stretches ahead and behind, indistinguishable, and I cannot say for certain which direction leads home.

A heaviness settles over everything here. It is the weight of loss, of regret—the money run out, gone before I understood how little remained. And there are the words, too, the terrible things I said to a child, sharp and thoughtless in the moment. I hold onto a fragile hope: that time might soften them, that they will be remembered as jokes rather than wounds, reframed by mercy I don't deserve.

I have come to notice how gestures and language slip into us almost without our knowing. A phrase, a way of moving the hands, a habit of speech—these enter our behavior imperceptibly, easing in *with less than a breath*. We become, without deciding to, an accumulation of everything we have absorbed from others.

I think of a student who once told me a story about bear hunting. He described how hunters use recordings of distressed animals—the cries of the wounded, the young in pain—to draw the bears out. It is illegal, this method, but brutally effective. The bears come to the sound of suffering, unable to resist the pull of it, and so their compassion becomes the very thing that betrays them.

Earlier, on the bus, I shared an apple with a child. A small thing—breaking the fruit, offering half, watching them take it. And in that moment I understood something about tenderness, about how far it asks us to travel. Love, I thought, is a long way to go. But perhaps these small acts are the road itself, the only way forward through the dark.
outputs.L4:
# Expanded Analysis

This poem explores themes of isolation, moral ambiguity, and human connection through its fragmented imagery of a speaker wandering alone at night beneath a "black moon." Rather than presenting a linear narrative, the work moves associatively, allowing the reader to piece together meaning from scattered impressions and half-articulated memories. The nocturnal setting establishes an atmosphere of uncertainty, where familiar moral distinctions blur and dissolve into shadow.

At the heart of the poem lies a deliberate interweaving of contradictory experiences. Memories of regret surface alongside recollections of predatory hunting practices, and both sit uneasily beside small, almost incidental acts of kindness. This structural choice reflects the poem's central preoccupation: the impossibility of separating our gentler impulses from our capacity for harm. The speaker does not offer these memories as confession or justification but rather as evidence of a self that contains multitudes, many of them irreconcilable.

The poem's power derives largely from its striking juxtapositions of tenderness and menace. In one moment, we witness the intimate gesture of sharing an apple with a child—an image of nourishment, trust, and simple human warmth. In another, we encounter the illegal luring of animals with distress calls, a practice that weaponizes the very sounds of suffering to draw victims closer. Placed side by side, these images resist easy interpretation. They insist that the same hands capable of offering sustenance are also capable of deception and violence.

Through this careful arrangement, the poem reveals how love and cruelty coexist within human experience, not as opposing forces locked in battle, but as intertwined aspects of a single, complicated nature. There is no clean resolution, no triumph of virtue over baseness. Instead, the reader is left to sit with the discomfort of recognizing both capacities within the speaker—and, by extension, within themselves.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that genuine connection is not easily achieved. It requires traversing a "long way" through darkness, moving through the very ambiguity and moral complexity the poem has laid bare. The black moon, offering no illumination, becomes a fitting emblem for this journey: connection must be sought not in the clarity of daylight certainties, but in the honest acknowledgment of our contradictions and the difficult, uncertain effort to reach one another despite them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem dedicated to someone named Alexander Moysaenko, using imagery of a black moon, birds, a dead phone, and a lonely road at night.
counterfactuals.output:
# For Alexander Moysaenko

The black moon hangs like a coin pressed into velvet, spending no light, and I am walking the road that has no end and no lamps, only the dark shapes of trees leaning in to listen.

Somewhere the birds have gone quiet—not asleep, Alexander, but waiting, the way birds wait before a storm they can feel in the small bones of their wings. I think of you in these long silences. I think of how the night keeps its promises when nothing else will.

My phone is a black stone in my hand. Dead. A little window into nothing, cracked with the map of some journey I can no longer read. So I hold it anyway, the way you hold a thing that used to speak, hoping warmth might wake it. It does not wake. The road unspools.

Alexander Moysaenko—your name a music I say aloud to keep the dark from closing over me completely. The syllables are stones I set down one by one, a path behind me that the night erases.

The black moon watches. The birds hold their breath in the branches like folded prayers. And I walk on, dead phone against my chest like a second heart that has forgotten how, down the lonely road that leads, I am certain now, to you—

or to the place where you once stood, luminous, before the moon turned black and swallowed all its gold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece of surreal poetry that jumps between disconnected scenes—a person alone on a dark road, a memory about a student who went bear hunting, and sharing an apple with a child on a bus.
counterfactuals.output:
**Provisions for the Journey**

The road has forgotten how to end.
I walk it anyway, my shadow
walking the wrong direction,
insisting on a sun I cannot verify.

---

Marcus went bear hunting in October.
He was nineteen and full of borrowed confidence,
told me in the margins of an essay
about Emerson, about self-reliance,
that he'd sleep in the woods with his grandfather's rifle
and come back changed.

He came back the same,
which was its own kind of transformation.
No bear. Just the story of a bear—
a brown movement between trees
that might have been weather.

I never graded that paper.
It's still ungraded somewhere,
a red pen hovering over the word *wilderness.*

---

On the bus a child asks for half my apple.
She doesn't ask, actually. She simply looks
with the negotiating eyes of the very small
and I am breaking the fruit against my knee
the way my father never taught me.

The white flesh browns immediately.
Everything begins to leave the moment you open it.

She eats the seeds. I let her.
Somewhere a tree is deciding whether to happen.

---

The road again. No streetlights,
only the idea of streetlights,
their absence hung like lamps.

I think: Marcus, did you want the bear
or the leaving-to-find-it?

I think: little girl, the apple
was never mine to begin with.

---

Here is what nobody explains—
how you can be three places at once
and lonely in all of them.
The dark road holds the bus
holds the classroom holds the woods
holds the bear that might be weather,
that might be a boy learning
the shape of his own hunger.

---

I offer the last piece to no one.
The road accepts it.
The road accepts everything eventually,

even me,

even the sun walking backward,
insisting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemporary free-verse prose poem with a fragmented, stream-of-consciousness style, opening with a dedication line and ending with the image "Get on your bike and ride through the lights."
counterfactuals.output:
*for everyone who left a city at 3 a.m. and called it healing*

The kettle again, the blue tick, the unread, the read-and-didn't-answer, the way morning arrives like a debt collector, polite until it isn't. I keep a list of things I meant to feel. Somewhere a fridge hums its one long vowel and I think this is prayer, this is the closest thing, the appliance liturgy, the standing in the fluorescent aisle deciding between two identical sadnesses in different packaging.

You said *later* like it was a place. I've been driving there for years.

Fragments — the sock without its brother, the password I changed and forgot, the mother's voice on a train platform saying *text me when you land*, as if landing were a promise anyone could keep. Half a sentence in my throat like a fishbone. The dog two floors down that barks at nothing, or at the exact right thing, at the weather coming, at the man who isn't home yet, at grief which has a smell, which the dog knows, which the dog always knew.

And still the body wants. Toast. Sunlight. The stranger's shoulder on the bus. To be touched without meaning. To mean without being touched.

I am trying to say I'm fine but the syntax keeps collapsing, the way a wave is fine right up until the shore, the way *fine* is four letters holding back a flood, the way you can love someone in past tense while they're still standing in your kitchen asking where you keep the spoons.

The lights change whether you're ready. Green means *go anyway*. Green means *the world will not wait for your permission*. Green means the intersection doesn't care about your fragments, your unread messages, your mother, your dog that isn't yours, your list of things you meant to feel and never did.

So do the animal thing. The stupid brave thing. The thing your legs remember when your head forgets.

Get on your bike and ride through the lights.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a dark, atmospheric poem addressed to an absent person. Include unsettling imagery like the "black heart of the moon," snakes, and hunters luring animals with recordings of distress.
counterfactuals.output:
**Absence, in the Key of Predation**

You left before the moon turned inward,
before it showed its black heart
like a stone swallowed and never passed—
and I have been listening for you
in the wrong frequencies since.

There are hunters in the far fields now.
They carry speakers into the dark
and play the recorded cries of the wounded,
the small distress of a fawn or a hare,
until the living come running
toward the sound of their own kind dying.

I understand this.
I have run toward such sounds myself.
I have mistaken your voice
for something that wanted to keep me.

The grass here holds its snakes
the way a sentence holds its meaning—
coiled, patient, waiting for the warmth
of anything foolish enough to lie down.
I lie down anyway.
I dream you back in pieces:
a wrist, a laugh, the cold turn of a shoulder.

The moon does not answer.
It only hangs there, hollowed,
a lure someone rigged in the sky
to draw the lonely upward and out.

And still I come when I am called.
And still I cannot tell the difference
between your name
and the noise a thing makes
when it is being taken.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something poetic and melancholic that blends longing, guilt about words said to a child, and strange rural memories, ending on a note about love being far away.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Fields Remember**

There were words I said to you once,
small and sharp as the first frost,
and I have carried them since
the way the barn carries its lean—
crooked, but still standing.

You were four, maybe five.
I told you the cold thing
because I was tired, because
the day had worn me down
to the grain of my own wood.

And you looked at me the way
the calves looked at the slaughter truck—
not yet knowing, only sensing
that the world had turned
some corner you couldn't see around.

I keep thinking of the rural strangeness:
the dead crow nailed to the fence post
that no one would admit to hanging,
the well that swallowed sound,
the summer the corn grew taller than the house
and my father wept for no reason
in the middle of all that green.

I wanted to raise you
in a place without such omens.
Instead I gave you my worst sentence,
handed it down like a family plot,
like the acreage of everything
we cannot take back.

Now the light goes long across the stubble.
Now the geese pull their gray thread south.
I would unsay it all
if the tongue could be forgiven,
if memory were a field
you could plow under.

But love, it seems,
is always somewhere else—
one county over,
past the flooded road,
in the lit window of a house
I keep meaning to reach
before the dark comes down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
